content: An Emergency Medical Technician-Intermediate (EMT-I) is a mid-level provider of prehospital emergency medical care in the United States. The role of an EMT-I is not to provide definitive medical care but to enhance prehospital critical care and deliver rapid on-scene treatment. EMT-Is are most commonly employed in ambulances, working alongside EMT-Basics and EMT-Paramedics. As a mid-level provider, EMT-Is are typically authorized to perform more advanced medical procedures than EMT-Basics and are trained to provide advanced life support. Education and Training EMT-I/85: The EMT-I/85 level of training allows for several invasive procedures beyond the basic level, such as intravenous (IV) therapy, the use of multi-lumen airway devices, and in some states, endotracheal intubation. EMT-I/85s also have enhanced assessment skills. However, they are generally limited to the same medications as EMT-Basics, including oxygen, oral glucose, activated charcoal, epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPens), nitroglycerin, and metered-dose inhalers (MDIs). In many states, they are also allowed to administer 5% and 50% dextrose in water (D5W and D50). Medication protocols vary by state. For example, in New Hampshire, EMT-Is can administer additional medications such as Narcan (naloxone), atropine, thiamine, and nebulized albuterol. EMT-I/99: The EMT-I/99 certification is the closest level to a Paramedic and allows for advanced techniques not available to EMT-I/85s. These include needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, endotracheal intubation, nasogastric tube placement, the use of cardiac event monitors/ECGs, and the administration of medications to manage certain cardiac arrhythmias. Higher Levels of EMTs Some states have additional specialized levels of EMT training beyond the national standards set by the U.S. Department of Transportation. These levels may have different names or expanded scopes of practice. Alaska: Alaska has EMT-II and EMT-III certifications. EMT-II is similar to the EMT-I/85 standard, while EMT-III is closer to the EMT-I/99 standard. A sponsoring physician can expand the scope of an EMT-III beyond state-defined protocols by providing additional training and quality control measures. This may include additional drugs and procedures, such as wound suturing. However, the EMT-III program is a short upgrade and does not generally receive reciprocity with other states. California: California uses the designation EMT-I (or EMT-One), which is equivalent to the National EMT-Basic level. This should not be confused with the EMT-Intermediate (EMT-I). Iowa: EMT-Basics in Iowa can administer EpiPens, insert Combi-Tubes, and set up and maintain non-medicated IVs, in addition to other basic skills. EMT-Intermediates can establish IVs and perform all EMT-Basic skills. Iowa Paramedics are certified as NREMT-Intermediate/99s, while the highest level of care in Iowa is the Paramedic Specialist, equivalent to the NREMT-Paramedic. Iowa also offers a Critical Care endorsement for Paramedic Specialists. Michigan: Michigan recognizes the DOT levels of EMT-B, EMT-I/85, and EMT-P but refers to EMT-I/85 as EMT-S (Specialist). However, as EMT-Basic standards approach the EMT-Paramedic level, the EMT-Specialist certification is being phased out. New York: New York State has an AEMT-CC (Advanced EMT-Critical Care) certification, which is unique to the state but nearly identical in curriculum to the national EMT-I/99 standard. New York also has an AEMT-I (Advanced EMT-Intermediate) certification, equivalent to the national EMT-I/85 standard. However, no advanced EMT certifications are recognized in New York City, where providers are either EMT-Basics or Paramedics. Oklahoma: Oklahoma previously recognized an EMT-Cardiac level, which has since been phased out. EMTs certified at this level have been retrained and certified as Paramedics or downgraded to EMT-I. Rhode Island: Rhode Island's first-level ALS providers are EMT-Cardiacs, a certification unique to Rhode Island and Virginia (though Virginia has recently phased out its Cardiac Tech program). EMT-Cardiacs can administer more cardiac drugs than EMT-Is but fewer than EMT-Ps. The EMT-Cardiac program is less time-intensive and costly than an EMT-P program and is widely used in Rhode Island fire departments, which provide the majority of EMS in the state. Tennessee: Tennessee licenses EMTs at either the EMT-IV (Intravenous Therapy) level or the EMT-Paramedic level. EMT-IVs are trained to the NREMT-B standard and receive additional training in advanced airway management, administration of epinephrine for anaphylaxis, nebulized beta-2 agonists (e.g., Xopenex, albuterol), D50W and D25W, IV therapy, and trauma life support, including the use of MAST trousers. EMT-IVs can also administer nitroglycerin, aspirin for cardiac emergencies, glucagon, and the Mark 1 Auto-Injector kit for organophosphate poisoning and suspected nerve gas exposure. The Tennessee Board of EMS is evaluating whether to allow EMT-IVs to administer Narcan and nitrous oxide and is considering transitioning to an EMT-B, EMT-Advanced, and EMT-P format, eliminating the EMT-IV rank. Vermont: Vermont's first level of ALS providers is the EMT-I '03, which is unique to the state. EMT-I '03s have an expanded scope of practice above EMT-I/85 but below EMT-I/99. They can provide IV therapy and administer medications such as albuterol, aspirin, D50, epinephrine (1:1000), glucagon, naloxone (Narcan), nitroglycerin, and thiamine, in addition to EMT-B level medications. Medical directors in each district can modify state protocols within their districts. Virginia: Virginia's first level of ALS is EMT-Enhanced, which is unique to the state. EMT-Enhanced providers can start IV lines, perform endotracheal intubation, perform chest decompressions, establish intraosseous (IO) lines, and administer medications such as D50, glucagon, albuterol/atrovent, epinephrine, and, in some cases, narcotics. Virginia has recently phased out its Cardiac Tech program. Wisconsin: Wisconsin offers an EMT-IV Technician certification for EMT-Basics, allowing them to start basic IV lines, treat hypovolemic shock, and administer Narcan, D5, and a limited number of other medications. This level of training is often used in non-urban areas where hospitals are sparse, and advanced life support intercepts or aero-medical transports may take significant time. Some private ambulance companies also employ EMT-IV Technicians for interfacility transports requiring IV therapy but not the specialized advanced care of a Paramedic, EMT-I, RN, or MD.
